q: For a straight conductor of length L carrying current I at right angles to a uniform field, the magnetic flux density is defined by:
x: From F = ILB sin 90° = ILB, the flux density is B = F/(IL), the force per unit current per unit length.

q: A 0.5 m wire carrying 2 A is placed at right angles to a uniform magnetic field and feels a force of 0.3 N. The flux density is:
x: B = F/(IL) = 0.3/(2 × 0.5) = 0.3 T. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 0.3 × 2 × 0.5, a different and wrong value.

q: A magnetic flux density of 0.02 T, expressed in gauss, is:
At a point in a magnetic field, the direction of the flux density vector is the direction in which:
o: A stationary positive charge would be pushed
The south pole of a small compass needle points
The north pole of a small compass needle points
x: B points along the field lines, the way a compass north pole points. A stationary charge feels no magnetic force, and the force on a wire is perpendicular to B.

q: Using F = qvB, the tesla can also be written as:
x: B = F/(qv), so its unit is N/(C × m s⁻¹) = N s C⁻¹ m⁻¹.

q: A current-carrying wire at right angles to a uniform field feels a force of 0.8 N. It is turned so that it makes 30° with the field, with the same current. The force becomes (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.87):
x: F = ILB sin θ. At 90° it is 0.8 N; at 30° it is 0.8 × sin 30° = 0.4 N. Using cos 30° gives about 0.7 N, which is wrong.

q: A wire lies at right angles to a uniform field. If both the current in it and its length inside the field are doubled, the force on it becomes:
x: F = ILB, so doubling both I and L multiplies the force by 2 × 2 = 4.

q: A uniform field B passes through a flat area A whose normal makes an angle θ with B. The magnetic flux through the area is:
x: Φ = B · A = BA cos θ, where θ is the angle between B and the normal (vector area). It is BA when the field is along the normal.

q: A square loop of side 20 cm is held with its plane at right angles to a uniform field of 0.5 T. The flux through it is:
x: A = 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.04 m², so Φ = BA = 0.5 × 0.04 = 0.02 Wb. Forgetting to square the side gives 0.1 Wb.

q: Magnetic flux density and vector area are both vectors, yet magnetic flux is a scalar. This is because flux is their:
x: The dot (scalar) product of two vectors gives a scalar: Φ = B · A. A cross product would give another vector.

q: The vector area of a flat surface is a vector whose magnitude is the area and whose direction is:
o: Along the surface, parallel to one edge
Along the normal to the surface
Along the tangent at the edge
x: Vector area points along the normal (perpendicular) to the plane of the surface. Its magnitude is the area.

q: Only 0.05 Wb of flux passes through a 0.2 m² coil placed in a 0.5 T field. What angle does the field make with the coil's normal? (cos 60° = 0.5)
x: Φ = BA cos θ gives cos θ = 0.05/(0.5 × 0.2) = 0.5, so θ = 60°.

q: A coil lies in a uniform field with its normal along the field, so the flux is BA. It is turned through 180°. The flux through it is now:
x: After a half turn the normal points opposite to B, so θ = 180° and Φ = BA cos 180° = −BA.

q: A loop has its normal along a uniform field. The field is doubled and the loop is tilted so its normal is at 60° to the field. The flux through the loop (cos 60° = 0.5):
x: New flux = 2B × A × cos 60° = 2B × A × 0.5 = BA, the same as before.

q: A charged particle moves in a circle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. The centripetal force it needs is supplied by the:
o: Magnetic force on the moving charge
Electric force from the magnet's poles
x: The magnetic force qvB is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it acts as the centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r.

q: The period of the circular motion of an ion of mass m and charge q circling in a uniform field B is:
x: T = 2πr/v and r = mv/(qB), so T = 2πm/(qB). The speed cancels out.

q: A charged particle moves in a circle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. As it goes round, its kinetic energy:
x: The magnetic force is perpendicular to the motion, so it does no work and the speed, hence kinetic energy, does not change.

q: In a mass spectrometer, an ion (2 × 10⁻²⁶ kg, 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) enters a 0.5 T field perpendicularly at 4 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Its circular path has radius:
A particle of charge q moves in a circle of radius r at right angles to a uniform field B. The magnitude of its momentum is:
x: From r = mv/(qB), the momentum mv = qBr.

q: A charged particle circles at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. Its speed and the flux density are both doubled. Compared with before, its radius and its period are:
x: r = mv/(qB): doubling v and B leaves r the same. T = 2πm/(qB) does not depend on v, so doubling B halves T.

q: Two ions with the same charge and the same speed enter a uniform magnetic field at right angles. The heavier ion moves in a circle that is:
o: Larger, because r is proportional to mass
Smaller, because r is inversely proportional to mass
The same size, because the charges are equal
Larger, because r is proportional to the square of mass
x: r = mv/(qB); with q, v and B equal, r is directly proportional to m. This is how a mass spectrometer separates ions.

q: The magnetic force on a charge moving through a uniform field is greatest when the angle between its velocity and the field is:
x: F = qvB sin θ is largest when sin θ = 1, at θ = 90°. At 0° and 180° the force is zero.

q: A positive charge moves towards the right across this page in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. The magnetic force on it is directed:
o: Towards the top of the page
Towards the bottom of the page
x: F = q(v × B). With v to the right and B into the page, v × B points towards the top of the page, and q is positive.

q: What force acts on an alpha particle (charge 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) travelling at 5 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a 0.2 T field?
x: F = qvB = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 5 × 10⁵ × 0.2 = 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁴ N. Using the charge of a single proton gives half this value.

q: A charged particle moving at right angles to a uniform field feels a force of 4 × 10⁻¹² N. At the same speed, moving at 30° to the field, it feels (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.87):
x: F = qvB sin θ, so the force falls to 4 × 10⁻¹² × sin 30° = 2 × 10⁻¹² N. Using cos 30° gives 3.5 × 10⁻¹², which is wrong.

q: A neutron moves at high speed at right angles to a strong uniform magnetic field. The magnetic force on it is:
o: Maximum, because it moves at 90° to the field
Along its velocity, speeding it up
Opposite to its velocity, slowing it down
Zero, because it has no charge
x: F = qvB sin θ and a neutron has q = 0, so it feels no magnetic force and moves straight on.

q: An electron moves vertically downward in a uniform horizontal magnetic field directed towards the north. The magnetic force on the electron is directed towards the:
x: For a positive charge, v (down) × B (north) points east. The electron is negative, so its force is reversed, towards the west.

q: The magnetic force on a moving charge can change the particle's:
o: Direction of motion but not its speed
x: The force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it only bends the path. It does no work, so the speed stays the same.
